analysis.one_liner: Lets homeowners with government-backed mortgages refinance at today's lower rates even if they owe more than their home is worth.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it was placed on the Senate calendar in September 2012 and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013, with no Republican cosponsor and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to expand their existing Home Affordable Refinance Program so that any homeowner current on a mortgage the two agencies own or guarantee could refinance at market rates, regardless of how little equity they had. It would have barred up-front fees, cut appraisal costs, let the agencies accept some borrower risk without extra charges to lenders, and required a public website where borrowers could check eligibility and see qualified lenders. It was introduced late in the session, placed on the Senate calendar, and never brought to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners whose mortgages are owned or guaranteed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac and who are current on their payments, especially those with little or no equity after the housing crash. They could refinance from above-market rates into lower ones without equity requirements, up-front fees, or full appraisal costs, and the bill required the loans to genuinely lower the payment, rate, or term.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Underwater homeowners with Fannie or Freddie loans

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the agencies to treat every current borrower as eligible for streamlined refinancing, and barred them from disqualifying borrowers or setting different rules based on loan-to-value, combined loan-to-value, employment status, or income.

It prohibited the agencies from charging lenders up-front fees such as loan-level price adjustments, and required alternative, streamlined valuation methods so that appraisal costs would not block refinancing; where automated valuation failed, the agencies themselves had to bear the cost of a manual appraisal.
The bill required refinanced loans to actually benefit the borrower through a lower payment, lower interest rate, a move to a more stable product such as a fixed rate, or a shorter term.

It required the agencies to notify every borrower with an agency-backed mortgage about the program, and required a single public website where borrowers could check eligibility, find qualified lenders, and calculate potential savings.

It directed the regulator to make the two agencies' refinancing guidelines consistent so lenders would not have to navigate two sets of rules, with a 90-day deadline for putting the changes into effect.

analysis.who_pays: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the federal backstop behind them take on more guarantee risk by refinancing loans with little or no equity. Investors holding higher-rate mortgage bonds would take losses when loans prepay. The bill tries to protect the treasury by locking guarantee fees at their April 2012 average and forbidding the agencies to offset the fee by cutting other charges.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fannie/Freddie, taxpayers backstopping them, mortgage bond investors

drawbacks.text: Refinancing loans with little or no equity into agency guarantees shifts more risk onto Fannie, Freddie, and ultimately the federal backstop. The bill's answer was to require the average guarantee fee on refinanced loans to be no lower than the April 1, 2012 average and to prohibit the agencies from offsetting that fee by lowering other charges, but the risk transfer itself remains.

Eligibility was limited: only borrowers current on their mortgage, with at most one late payment in the prior year, on first mortgages originated or refinanced on or before May 31, 2009. Homeowners already behind on payments were excluded.

A wave of refinancing of above-market-rate loans would have imposed prepayment losses on investors in those mortgage-backed securities, which is a standard cost of rate-driven refinancing but a real one for that group.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For homeowners trapped in above-market rates on agency-backed loans, the savings would have been direct and substantial, and the bill was built around an existing program rather than a new one. The main honest objections are the added risk on the agencies' books and the losses to mortgage bond investors; the bill addressed the first with a fee floor and offset prohibition, and the second is the ordinary cost of allowing people to refinance. On balance a help to ordinary homeowners with a real but managed cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2012, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on September 10, 2012 with twelve Senate colleagues as original cosponsors.
It was read a second time on September 11, 2012 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 503, a step short of floor consideration.
No further action appears in the record: no committee markup, no motion to proceed, no floor debate, and no vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or an independent; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homeowners with agency-backed mortgages kept paying pre-crisis interest rates, and investors in those higher-rate mortgage loans kept their above-market yields. The agencies' books also stayed as they were. With the Congress over, the bill is dead.

for.name: Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor.

for.name: 21 of 51 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining one independent, giving it 22 backers, all from the Democratic caucus.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar from September 2012 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats plus one independent, and the action history shows no Republican support and no floor vote; the bill never reached the point where party splits would show up in a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have directed them to guarantee a wave of refinanced loans with little or no equity, adding risk to their books and the federal backstop behind them, while the fee floor tried to preserve their revenue. As government-seized companies, their gains and losses land partly on taxpayers.

Mass refinancing of above-market-rate agency loans would have caused prepayments that cut those investors' yields. Their interest in blocking refinancing runs directly against homeowners' interest in lower payments.

The bill removes up-front agency fees, narrows the representations and warranties lenders must stand behind, and harmonizes the two agencies' rules, cutting lender costs while expanding refinance volume. Lenders profit from more refinancing at the same time homeowners save.
